title: Extreme Ownership
coreMove: accept responsibility at the level where repair becomes possible, then change the procedures and communication that shaped the result
sourcePressure: The namesake chapter uses the Ramadi friendly-fire failure to show a leader refusing excuses and owning the system that produced the failure.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: take the blame publicly and move on

sourceAnchors.name: Jocko Willink
sourceAnchors.detail: the source says he treats the Ramadi blue-on-blue incident as a leadership problem he has to own instead of spreading blame through chaos
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Jocko Willink’s move is not a speech about guilt; he keeps responsibility close enough to the failure that repair can begin.

sourceAnchors.name: Ramadi blue-on-blue incident
sourceAnchors.detail: the source describes it as chaotic, involving incomplete information and many people, yet still used to show ownership instead of excuse-making
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The blue-on-blue failure matters because it offers every reasonable excuse, and ownership refuses to start there.

counterintuition: leadership is harder than it looks
tryThisNow: ask yourself how to be a better leader

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital specimen lab after a mislabeled blood tube reaches processing
exampleSpecs.audience: a lab supervisor facing angry nurses and a shaken technician
exampleSpecs.stakes: a patient result could be tied to the wrong person if the chain is not repaired
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor says the miss belongs to her process, marks the unclear handoff on the accession log, and changes the two-person check before the next batch
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a red-top blood tube lies beside an accession label with one digit wrong

exampleSpecs.domain: regional airport baggage desk after mobility equipment is sent to the wrong city
exampleSpecs.audience: a baggage operations lead with agents blaming the connecting carrier
exampleSpecs.stakes: a passenger lands without essential equipment and the desk loses trust
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lead stops the carrier blame, walks to the transfer tag printer, finds the missing exception step, and assigns a manual verification for mobility items
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You are close enough to see this: torn transfer tag curls from the edge of a stalled baggage belt.
mustAvoid: airline complaint scene about rude customers

exampleSpecs.domain: cybersecurity incident from an old contractor account
exampleSpecs.audience: an IT director briefing executives after a limited breach
exampleSpecs.stakes: leaders may blame one analyst instead of closing the access-control gap
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director opens with my offboarding process failed, shows the stale account in the access report, and commits to a weekly owner review
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The first thing you register is physical: stale contractor username glows amber on an access-review report.

exampleSpecs.domain: artisan bakery after sesame cross-contact in a nut-free order
exampleSpecs.audience: a bakery owner managing a frightened parent and defensive bakers
exampleSpecs.stakes: a food-allergy trust breach can close wholesale accounts
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner traces the failure to unlabeled cooling racks, relabels allergen zones before reopening, and personally briefs the staff on the changed flow
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Hold there," someone says. Sesame seeds cling to parchment under a tray marked for the wrong order.

exampleSpecs.domain: city snow removal after one cul-de-sac is missed twice
exampleSpecs.audience: a public works foreman with drivers blaming an outdated route file
exampleSpecs.stakes: residents are trapped on an icy hill and council pressure is rising
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the foreman owns the route-control miss, pins the omitted street on the dispatch wall, and requires drivers to mark exceptions before leaving the yard
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Later, the team will trace the lesson back to this: pink street tab hangs crooked on a laminated snow route wall.

exampleSpecs.domain: nonprofit gala check-in after donor QR codes fail
exampleSpecs.audience: an event director with volunteers blaming the ticketing vendor
exampleSpecs.stakes: major donors wait in a line long enough to sour the evening
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director tells the volunteer lead the backup table was her responsibility, opens the printed guest binder, and moves three people to handwritten check-in
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What changes once this is in front of everyone: locked phone stand displays a spinning QR code at the ballroom entrance?

skillTargets: separate owning the system from taking symbolic blame
spot excuse patterns that prevent repair
choose a procedure or communication change after failure

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one recent miss and write the condition you controlled that made it easier, then name the one process change you can make before the next attempt.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following 'concrete anchor -> abstract rule -> elaboration'
